september-5-2024.gazette: ABC Sports arrived in Munich in 1972 to cover swimming and track, and by the second week its control room was running the first live hostage crisis on television. The film reconstructs that room decision by decision — the chain of command under Roone Arledge, the argument for keeping the story on the sports feed, the unconfirmed report of a rescue that went out to the world before it was corrected. The drama is procedural, and the subject is what a broadcast does with a fact it does not yet have.

the-voice-of-hind-rajab-2025.gazette: The Palestine Red Crescent Society kept the tape. A dispatcher in Ramallah stayed on the line for hours with a five-year-old girl trapped in a shot-up car in Gaza City in January 2024, while an ambulance tried to reach her. Kaouther Ben Hania built the film around that recording rather than a reenactment of it; Hind Rajab and the two paramedics sent for her were found dead in the wreckage.

warfare-2025.gazette: Ray Mendoza was a Navy SEAL in Ramadi in 2006, and Warfare is his reconstruction of a single overwatch mission that went wrong, made with Alex Garland out of his memory and his platoon-mates'. The film holds to something close to real time, with no briefing, no aftermath, and almost no music. What it preserves instead is procedure — radio protocol, casualty handling, the interval between an explosion and anyone knowing who is hurt.
warfare-2025.prism: Building from memory buys precision inside the house and forfeits everything outside it — the radio traffic is exact to the second, the Iraqi family in the other room is barely a fact. That's the trade: a war rendered so carefully that why anyone is there never has to come up.

le-trou-1960.gazette: The escape from La Santé in 1947 happened, and the man at the center of Becker's frame was in it — Jean Keraudy plays a version of the prisoner who planned it, and handles the tools himself on camera. Whole stretches of the film are just labor: concrete cut through by hand, a periscope built from a toothbrush and mirror glass, floorboards lifted at the pace the work actually took. Becker died before it reached cinemas.

when-a-woman-ascends-the-stairs-1960.gazette: Naruse's Ginza runs on arithmetic. A hostess buys her own kimono, carries her customers' unpaid tabs, and is expected to raise capital from the men she entertains if she ever wants a bar of her own. The film keeps that ledger in view and treats aging as an actuarial problem, which makes the nightlife district look less like a pleasure quarter than a thin-margin industry.

pigs-and-battleships-1961.gazette: Yokosuka's base town supported an economy of its own at the end of the 1950s — bars, brokers, and in Imamura's telling a gang fattening pigs on garbage hauled out of the American naval base. He crowds the frame in deep focus so nobody is ever alone in it; a hustler is always somebody's cousin, a woman is always somebody's earner. The pigs get into the streets before the film is over.
pigs-and-battleships-1961.prism: Shooting the underclass this densely also turns it into spectacle — the swarm that makes Yokosuka feel real is the same device that never lets one person hold a quiet shot. And the pigs are the argument: the town lives on what the base throws out, and the stampede is that arrangement getting loose.

the-insect-woman-1963.gazette: Imamura opens on an insect hauling itself over a clod of earth, then files the rest like a case record, with intertitles stamping the years and freeze-frames stopping the action mid-gesture. A woman's life runs from a tenant farm in the northeast to a Tokyo brothel and back to the fields, and the silk work, the tenancy, the wartime factory, and the sex trade all arrive as economics rather than misfortune. The research shows in what the film declines to dramatize.

dr-strangelove-1964.gazette: Kubrick read the deterrence literature before he wrote the jokes — RAND papers, fail-safe procedure, Herman Kahn's arithmetic of megadeaths, from which the doomsday machine is lifted nearly intact. The Air Force declined to cooperate, so the B-52 interior was reconstructed from published material, and the complaint afterward was that it looked too much like the real thing. The satire's premises were the doctrine's premises, unaltered.

army-of-shadows-1969.gazette: Melville had served with the Free French, and Kessel wrote the source novel in London in 1943 while the networks it described were still running. The film treats resistance as clerical, fatal work — forged papers, timetables, an informer killed by hand in a rented room because a gunshot would carry to the neighbors. It opened in 1969, a year after the barricades, and French critics read its gravity as Gaullism; it waited nearly forty years for an American release.
army-of-shadows-1969.prism: The Gaullism charge landed partly because 1969 wanted the Resistance either heroic or hypocritical, and Melville filed it as administration — dull, lethal, on schedule. What he protects is not the myth but the people inside it, which is harder to argue with and much harder to sell.

f-for-fake-1973.gazette: Welles started from footage of Elmyr de Hory, the forger whose paintings were hanging in museums under other men's names, and of Clifford Irving, who had written the book about him. Mid-production Irving was exposed for forging Howard Hughes's autobiography, and the film absorbed the second hoax into the first. Welles opens by guaranteeing that everything in the next hour is true, and the film runs longer than an hour.

mirror-1975.gazette: Mirror does not imitate newsreel; it uses it — Soviet troops dragging equipment through the shallows of Lake Sivash in 1943, Spanish children put onto evacuation ships, a stratospheric balloon, the Chinese border. Tarkovsky cut the archive against his own family's rooms and graded both to the same weight, so a mother at a printing press and a state's war footage carry equally. He said the cameraman who shot the Sivash crossing was killed soon after filming it.

the-travelling-players-1975.gazette: A theatre troupe crosses Greece between 1939 and 1952 trying to get through a nineteenth-century pastoral called Golfo the Shepherdess, and history interrupts every performance — the Metaxas dictatorship, the German occupation, the December fighting in Athens, the civil war, the camps. Angelopoulos shot it in long takes as the colonels' censorship regime came apart, and set the Oresteia's plot of betrayal and reckoning inside the documented years. The play is never finished.
the-travelling-players-1975.prism: Running the civil war through the Oresteia gives the losing side a shape the Greek state would not grant it, and turns politics into family fate at the same time. Angelopoulos took that trade because in 1975 the left's account of those years still had almost no official standing.

soldier-of-orange-1977.gazette: Erik Hazelhoff Roelfzema wrote the memoir and Verhoeven kept its shape — Leiden students in 1938, then an occupation that sorts them one at a time into collaborators, casualties, and couriers crossing to London by sea. The resistance here carries no romance; the betrayals are domestic, the radio work gets people arrested, and Queen Wilhelmina's government-in-exile is a suite of rooms with protocol in them. The hero comes through largely on luck and connections.

apocalypse-now-1979.gazette: The helicopters were Philippine Air Force machines on loan, recalled from the set at intervals to fight an actual insurgency in the south. A typhoon flattened the sets, Martin Sheen had a heart attack at thirty-six, and the burning treeline was thousands of gallons of gasoline detonated for the camera. Hearts of Darkness later released the footage Eleanor Coppola was shooting while all of it happened, which is why the production has never separated from the film.

kagemusha-1980.gazette: Takeda Shingen died in 1573 and his house kept it quiet for three years, which is the historical fact Kurosawa builds the double on. The film ends at Nagashino in 1575, where Oda and Tokugawa gunners behind palisades broke the Takeda cavalry, and Kurosawa stages the defeat as sound and aftermath — the charge rides out, and what the camera returns to is a field of dying horses. The clan the double stood in for was gone within a decade.
kagemusha-1980.prism: The double works because a warlord is a banner, a silhouette, and a seat — which is the least flattering possible description of the order he holds together. Then the guns at Nagashino settle it from the other direction, making the great man and his stand-in equally beside the point.
